name: Bakhtiyarpur–Panikoili Highway
aka: Formed from parts of the former NH 31, NH 33 and NH 215
lanes: Four lanes between Barhi, Hazaribagh, Ramgarh and Ranchi; two lanes on several other stretches

timeline.event: Given the number NH 20 in the national highway renumbering, joining parts of the old NH 31, NH 33 and NH 215
The four-lane Hazaribagh–Ramgarh–Ranchi section, often called the Ranchi–Hazaribagh Expressway, is completed

history: NH 20 runs from Bakhtiyarpur on the Ganga in Bihar down to Panikoili in Odisha, crossing the hills and forests of the Chota Nagpur plateau on the way. It was created in the 2010 renumbering of national highways by joining older roads, including parts of the old NH 31, NH 33 and NH 215. South of Nawada the road leaves the flat Ganga plains and climbs the Rajauli ghat onto the plateau, entering mining country around Koderma and Hazaribagh. The busiest and best-built part is the four-lane stretch from Barhi through Hazaribagh and Ramgarh to Ranchi, finished in 2012 with a bypass at Hazaribagh town. Beyond Ranchi the highway threads through Chandil, Chaibasa and the iron-ore hills of Kendujhar before ending on NH 16, the Kolkata–Chennai coastal highway.
facts: About 729 km long, crossing Bihar, Jharkhand and Odisha.
Meets the historic Grand Trunk Road corridor at Barhi in Jharkhand.
Ranchi, the capital of Jharkhand, is the biggest city on the route.
Passes the famous Maa Tarini temple at Ghatagaon in Odisha.
Ends at Panikoili on NH 16, the Kolkata–Chennai coastal highway.
The Barhi–Hazaribagh–Ramgarh–Ranchi stretch is a four-lane road widely known as the Ranchi–Hazaribagh Expressway.
It runs through two famous mineral belts — the mica mines around Koderma and the iron-ore hills of Kendujhar.
The Rajauli ghat, south of Nawada, is where the road climbs off the Ganga plains onto the Chota Nagpur plateau.
significance: NH 20 is the main road link between the crowded Ganga plains of Bihar and the mineral belt of Jharkhand and Odisha. Trucks carrying iron ore, coal and mica use it every day, and it gives central Bihar its most direct road to Ranchi and onward to the Odisha coast. For the many small hill and forest towns along the way it is the only proper all-weather road they have.

travelNotes: End to end is a long 14–16 hour drive, so most people break the journey at Ranchi, which sits roughly halfway. The plateau stretches through Koderma, Chandil and Kendujhar are hilly, forested and thinly settled, and local drivers prefer to cover them in daylight. Truck traffic from the mines is heaviest between Kendujhar and Panikoili. The monsoon, from June to September, brings mist and slippery ghat bends; October to February is the pleasant season.
futureUpgrades: The Bakhtiyarpur–Rajauli stretch in Bihar is being four-laned by NHAI in several packages.
The Kendujhar–Panikoili stretch in Odisha is also being four-laned.
